plan: Complete enhanced-ACT social-science passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000045, 'Language Nests'), about 590 words, including the Hebrew revival as the best-known precedent, on language endangerment and revitalization (Māori kōhanga reo from 1982, Hawaiian immersion, the home as the decisive setting, parents learning as adults). Topic checked against all ACT Reading and SAT R&W passages (no revitalization passage). Figures hedged ('linguists estimate', 'relatively few', 'were thought to'). 10 questions. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: R045-01 medium→easy, R045-05 medium→easy, R045-06 medium→easy, R045-07 hard→easy, R045-08 medium→easy, R045-09 medium→easy, R045-10 hard→medium.

passages.title: Language Nests
passages.text:
Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, linguists estimate that about 40 percent are endangered, meaning that fewer and fewer children are learning them. When the last speakers of a language die, a way of naming the world can disappear with them, along with songs, stories, and knowledge of local plants and places.

For a long time, many observers assumed that this process could not be reversed. Once parents stopped speaking a language to their children, the thinking went, the language was on a one-way path to silence. Several communities have since challenged that assumption.

The best-known example is Hebrew. For many centuries it was used mainly in prayer, scholarship, and writing rather than in everyday conversation. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, families and schools in what is now Israel began using it as a language of the home and the classroom, and today it has millions of native speakers. Other communities, facing far greater odds, have tried to follow a similar path.

In New Zealand, the Māori language declined sharply during the twentieth century, as many Māori families moved to cities and children were discouraged from speaking it in school. By the 1970s, surveys found that relatively few Māori children could speak it. In 1982, Māori communities began opening kōhanga reo, or "language nests": preschools in which elders spoke only Māori with young children throughout the day. Within a decade, hundreds of nests had opened, and many graduates went on to Māori-language primary schools. A similar approach was adopted in Hawaiʻi, where by the early 1980s fewer than fifty children were thought to speak Hawaiian as a first language.

These programs share a central idea: a language survives only if children use it, and children learn a language most fully when they hear it early and often. Adult classes, dictionaries, and recordings all matter, but they cannot by themselves make a language part of daily life. Researchers who study revitalization often point to the home as the decisive setting. A language that children hear at school but never at the dinner table may become something they know about rather than something they speak.

That is why revitalization is so difficult. Many parents in endangered-language communities never learned the language themselves; they must learn it as adults before they can pass it on, often while working and raising families. Even so, the results so far suggest that the outcome is not fixed. Languages that once seemed to be fading have gained new young speakers, not because of laws or scholarship alone, but because families decided to speak them.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Laws and dictionaries have proven to be the most effective ways to save endangered languages around the world.
choices.B: Some communities have shown that endangered languages can gain new speakers, mainly by reaching young children, though the work is hard.
choices.C: Most of the world's endangered languages will disappear within a decade no matter what communities attempt.
choices.D: The Māori language was never truly endangered, since many adults continued to speak it throughout the twentieth century.

candidates.evidence: the results so far suggest that the outcome is not fixed
candidates.explanation: The passage challenges the idea that language loss is irreversible, describes child-focused programs that have produced new speakers, and acknowledges the difficulty.

A.rationale: The passage says such tools cannot by themselves make a language part of daily life.

C.rationale: The passage argues the outcome "is not fixed" and describes languages gaining speakers.

D.rationale: The passage says the language declined sharply and few children could speak it by the 1970s.

hints: What assumption does the passage challenge, and what does it conclude?
candidates.remember: A main idea must include both the claim and its qualification.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, a language is described as endangered when:

choices.A: it has no written alphabet or dictionary.
choices.B: its speakers have moved from rural areas to cities.
choices.C: it is no longer taught in any school.
choices.D: fewer and fewer children are learning it.

candidates.evidence: meaning that fewer and fewer children are learning them
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines endangered languages as those that "fewer and fewer children are learning."

A.rationale: The passage does not define endangerment by writing.

B.rationale: Moving to cities is one cause of decline for Māori, not the definition of endangered.

C.rationale: The passage defines endangerment by children learning the language, not by schooling.

strategy.explanation: Look for the definition right after the term.

candidates.remember: Definitions often follow words like "meaning" or "that is."

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 1, which of the following can disappear when the last speakers of a language die?

choices.A: songs, stories, and knowledge of local plants and places
choices.B: the written records kept by linguists who studied the language
choices.C: the laws that once protected the language in schools
choices.D: the dictionaries and recordings made during revival efforts

candidates.evidence: along with songs, stories, and knowledge of local plants and places
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says that when the last speakers die, a way of naming the world can disappear, "along with songs, stories, and knowledge of local plants and places."

B.rationale: The passage does not say linguists' records disappear.

C.rationale: No such laws are mentioned in paragraph 1.

D.rationale: Dictionaries and recordings are mentioned later as tools, not as things that disappear.

hints: Find what disappears "along with" the language.
candidates.remember: Detail questions are answered by a specific sentence; ignore tools mentioned later.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, kōhanga reo were:

choices.A: adult evening classes that taught Māori grammar.
choices.B: government offices that recorded the speech of elders.
choices.C: preschools in which elders spoke only Māori with young children.
choices.D: primary schools that taught partly in English and partly in Māori.

candidates.evidence: preschools in which elders spoke only Māori with young children throughout the day
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes kōhanga reo as "preschools in which elders spoke only Māori with young children throughout the day."

A.rationale: The nests were preschools for young children, not adult classes.

B.rationale: Recordings are mentioned only generally; the nests were preschools.

D.rationale: The nests were preschools using only Māori; primary schools came afterward.

hints: Find the description after the colon in paragraph 4.
candidates.remember: Check each part of the description: who, where, and in what language.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 5, the word "decisive" most nearly means:

choices.A: quick to make up one's mind and act.
choices.B: most important in determining the result.
choices.C: final and impossible to change later.
choices.D: easy to identify or point out.

candidates.evidence: point to the home as the decisive setting
candidates.explanation: The paragraph argues that home use determines whether a language is spoken, so "decisive" means most important in determining the result.

A.rationale: That familiar meaning describes a person, but here the word describes a setting.

C.rationale: The sentence does not say the home is unchangeable.

D.rationale: The word concerns importance, not ease of identification.

hints: What role does the paragraph give the home?

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own.

candidates.remember: When a word usually describes people, check how it applies to a thing.

candidates.stem: The mention of Hawaiʻi at the end of paragraph 4 mainly serves to:

choices.A: prove that Hawaiian is now spoken by more children than Māori is.
choices.B: explain why Māori families moved to cities in the twentieth century.
choices.C: suggest that the Hawaiian language had already disappeared by 1980.
choices.D: show that the language-nest approach was used beyond New Zealand.

candidates.evidence: A similar approach was adopted in Hawaiʻi
candidates.explanation: The sentence says a similar approach was adopted in Hawaiʻi, extending the Māori example to another community.

A.rationale: The passage makes no such comparison.

B.rationale: Hawaiʻi is not connected to the Māori migration.

C.rationale: Fewer than fifty children spoke it, but it had not disappeared.

strategy.explanation: Connect the sentence to the example before it.

candidates.remember: A second example usually shows that a point applies more widely.

candidates.subskill: Applying a claim to a case
candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 5, a child who studies an endangered language at school but never hears it at home would most likely:

choices.A: become a more fluent speaker than a child who hears it only at home.
choices.B: refuse to learn the language because it is taught only at school.
choices.C: know a good deal about the language without using it in everyday life.
choices.D: lose the ability to speak the community's other languages.

candidates.evidence: may become something they know about rather than something they speak
candidates.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 5 warns that a language heard at school but not at home may become something children know about rather than speak.

A.rationale: The paragraph treats the home, not school, as the decisive setting.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests children refuse to learn it.

D.rationale: The paragraph says nothing about losing other languages.

hints: What does paragraph 5 say about school-only exposure?

strategy.explanation: Apply the final sentence of paragraph 5.

candidates.remember: Apply the passage's stated claim directly to the new case.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, one reason revitalization is difficult is that:

choices.A: many parents must first learn the language themselves as adults.
choices.B: children learn new languages less easily than adults do.
choices.C: many communities lack enough elders to staff language nests.
choices.D: governments have refused to allow the languages to be taught in schools.

candidates.evidence: they must learn it as adults before they can pass it on
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 6 explains that many parents never learned the language and must learn it as adults before passing it on.

B.rationale: The passage says children learn most fully when they hear a language early, the opposite.

C.rationale: This may sound plausible, but the passage never gives it as a reason.

D.rationale: The passage mentions no such refusal; Māori-language schools exist.

hints: Find "That is why revitalization is so difficult."

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence after the claim.

candidates.remember: A reason usually follows a claim like "That is why..."

candidates.stem: According to the passage, which of the following contributed to the decline of the Māori language in the twentieth century?

choices.A: The closing of the kōhanga reo and of the Māori-language primary schools
choices.B: A law that made Māori the only language allowed in New Zealand's schools
choices.C: A decision by many elders to speak only English with their grandchildren
choices.D: Families moving to cities and children being discouraged from speaking it in school

candidates.evidence: as many Māori families moved to cities and children were discouraged from speaking it in school
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 names two causes: families moving to cities and children being discouraged from speaking Māori in school.

A.rationale: These schools opened as part of the revival, not the decline.

B.rationale: No such law is mentioned; children were discouraged from speaking Māori in school.

C.rationale: The passage does not mention any such decision.

strategy.explanation: Read the clause that follows "declined sharply."

candidates.remember: Cause questions are answered by the reasons the passage lists.

candidates.stem: Within the passage as a whole, the example of Hebrew in paragraph 3 mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why Hebrew is far more widely spoken today than either the Māori or the Hawaiian language is.
choices.B: provide an established case showing that the assumption described in paragraph 2 can be wrong.
choices.C: argue that language revitalization can succeed only when a new country is founded.
choices.D: show that languages used mainly in prayer are much less likely to become endangered.

candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes the belief that language loss cannot be reversed and says communities have challenged it; Hebrew, revived as an everyday home language, is offered as the best-known counterexample.

A.rationale: The passage does not compare how widely the three languages are spoken.

C.rationale: The passage never ties success to founding a country; it credits families and schools.

D.rationale: The passage does not make any claim about prayer and endangerment.

hints: What assumption comes right before the Hebrew example?

strategy.explanation: Connect paragraph 3 to the claim at the end of paragraph 2.

candidates.remember: An example placed right after a claim usually supports or illustrates it.

revision_log.reason: Round-1 blind solves matched every key with no blocking flags; both noted that R045-01 and R045-10 (author's attitude) tested the same 'real success but hard' point and cued each other, and that R045-08's distractors were implausible. Replaced 10 with an item on the function of the Hebrew example and gave 08 plausible but unsupported distractors. Passage unchanged. Whole batch re-solved blind.

Round-2 solves matched every key with no blocking flags; both noted that the new R045-10 (function of the Hebrew example) and R045-03 (function of paragraph 2) tested the same point and cued each other. Replaced 03 with a paragraph-1 detail item. Re-solved blind.
